article_title: Computational Thinking for a Computational World
citation: Digital Promise. (2017). Computational Thinking for a Computational World. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: K-12 Computer Science Framework's seven core practices with computational thinking at the heart
description: The paper reports that the K-12 Computer Science Framework, published in 2016 by the ACM, CSTA, Code.org, and more than 100 experts, identifies seven core practices of computer science: fostering an inclusive computing culture, collaborating around computing, recognizing and defining computational problems, developing and using abstractions, creating computational artifacts, testing and refining computational artifacts, and communicating about computing. "The framework places computational thinking at the heart of the seven core practices, identifying practices 3 through 6 as components of computational thinking and practices 1, 2 and 7 as complementary." This positions computational thinking as core to computer science while extending beyond it.
requirements: Practices 3 through 6 are treated as components of computational thinking within computer science education
examples: The paper reproduces the framework's practice diagram showing practices 3–6 at the center surrounded by practices 1, 2, and 7
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2017). Computational Thinking for a Computational World. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/a84a9ab5-6541-417f-ba96-4a66715e7732

article_title: Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career
citation: Luna, C., & Weisgrau, J. (2025, March). Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/244
title: Design K-12 environments so learners make decisions, explore interests, and reflect, cultivating personal agency
description: The report argues learners need a sense of personal agency to actively participate in their learning journey, make informed decisions, and manage uncertainty, and that schools are uniquely positioned to foster this by creating environments where learners can explore, make decisions, and reflect on their learning. It recommends flexible learning pathways, learner-led conferences and portfolio reviews, and shifting teachers from keepers of knowledge to coaches. Practices should complement, not replace, tests and grades.
requirements: Investment in universal early childhood education programs designed with agency in mind
educator role shifts toward coaching learners in lifelong-learning mindsets
constraints: Many social structures, including socioeconomic status and educational attainment, impact an individual's ability to develop and exert their full sense of agency
examples: Synergy High School in Mineola, New York was co-designed with students to facilitate interactive learning, digital badges, and self-directed spaces, and the district found the model worked particularly well for students who had struggled in less autonomous environments
key_sources: Luna, C., & Weisgrau, J. (2025, March). Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/244

article_title: Ticket to Nowhere: The Gap between Leaving High School and Entering College and High-Performance Jobs.
citation: Haycock, Kati, Ed.; Barth, Patte, Ed.; Mitchell, Ruth, Ed.; Wilkins, Amy, Ed. (1999). Ticket to Nowhere: The Gap between Leaving High School and Entering College and High-Performance Jobs. Thinking K-16; v3 n2 Fall 1999. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED457262
title: The K-16 Square: four interlocking commitments linking K-12 and higher education to bring all students to high standards
description: The K-16 Square is a framework drafted by state education CEOs from seven states (with the National Association of System Heads and the Education Trust) representing four interlocking and equally important commitments as the corners of a figure: ensure all high school graduates meet high standards; accept only teachers who can bring all students' performance to high standards; accept into college only students who meet high standards; and ensure all teacher candidates produced are prepared to bring student performance to high standards. The framework holds that "Change in one sector cannot be accomplished without change in the others," with standards for K-12 graduation congruent with college admission standards. The CEOs propose that about a third of states achieve the universal goal by 2010 and the rest by 2020.
requirements: Strong interaction among sectors: standards for graduation must be congruent with standards for college admission, and teacher preparation standards congruent with school employment standards
Publicly available, accurate data on the performance of schools, colleges, universities and their students
constraints: Each state must establish its own timetable because socioeconomic and political circumstances vary and may change suddenly
target_learners: all K-12 and college students, especially low-income and minority students
target_learning_goals: meeting high achievement standards from elementary through postsecondary education, preparation for work and citizenship
examples: The CEOs' statement cites El Paso, Texas, where a five-year collaboration between higher education, K-12, and community leaders raised academic performance for all students and reduced the minority achievement gap by about two-thirds
key_sources: Haycock, Kati, Ed.; Barth, Patte, Ed.; Mitchell, Ruth, Ed.; Wilkins, Amy, Ed. (1999). Ticket to Nowhere: The Gap between Leaving High School and Entering College and High-Performance Jobs. Thinking K-16; v3 n2 Fall 1999. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED457262

article_title: K12-KGraph: A Curriculum-Aligned Knowledge Graph for Benchmarking and Training Educational LLMs
citation: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Mingrui Chen, Hengyi Feng, Zhaoyang Han, Xiaochen Ma, Zhen Hao Wong, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Wentao Zhang. (2026). K12-KGraph: A Curriculum-Aligned Knowledge Graph for Benchmarking and Training Educational LLMs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09635
title: K12-KGraph: a curriculum-aligned knowledge graph built from official Chinese K-12 textbooks
description: K12-KGraph is a heterogeneous property graph extracted from official People's Education Press textbooks covering mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology across primary, middle, and high school. It has "nine node types (Book, Chapter, Section, Concept, Skill, Experiment, Exercise, Figure, VisualElement)" and fourteen relation types spanning curriculum structure and visual grounding. Construction uses a five-stage pipeline with OCR parsing, LLM extraction, hierarchical merging, and DAG validation, with all triples manually verified by domain experts.
requirements: Edges carry confidence and evidence fields linking back to underlying textbook excerpts; all extracted triples are manually verified by domain experts
constraints: Grounded in the official Chinese People's Education Press curriculum; covers mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology only
target_learners: K-12 students in Chinese primary, middle, and high school
target_learning_goals: Curriculum cognition: prerequisite chains, concept taxonomies, experiment-concept links, and pedagogical sequencing
examples: The graph was built by prompting GPT-5.2 per section with a schema-aware instruction, then merging per-section graphs bottom-up and running depth-first cycle detection on the is_a and prerequisites_for subgraphs
key_sources: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Mingrui Chen, Hengyi Feng, Zhaoyang Han, Xiaochen Ma, Zhen Hao Wong, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Wentao Zhang. (2026). K12-KGraph: A Curriculum-Aligned Knowledge Graph for Benchmarking and Training Educational LLMs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09635

article_title: K12-KGraph: A Curriculum-Aligned Knowledge Graph for Benchmarking and Training Educational LLMs
citation: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Mingrui Chen, Hengyi Feng, Zhaoyang Han, Xiaochen Ma, Zhen Hao Wong, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Wentao Zhang. (2026). K12-KGraph: A Curriculum-Aligned Knowledge Graph for Benchmarking and Training Educational LLMs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09635
title: K12-Bench: a 23,640-question multi-select benchmark of graph-derived curriculum-cognition tasks
description: K12-Bench converts graph textual neighborhoods into multi-select questions for evaluating LLMs' curriculum cognition. It contains "23,640 multi-select items in total" grouped into five task families: Ground, Prereq, Neighbor, Evidence, and Locate. Questions and distractors are graph-derived rather than LLM-generated, and models receive only the question text without graph context, so the benchmark probes parametric curriculum knowledge. A stratified spot-check found 98.4% of sampled items fully correct.
requirements: Gold answers derive deterministically from validated K12-KGraph subgraphs, so benchmark quality depends on graph quality
constraints: Multi-select format with gold answer cardinality from 1 to 3; probes parametric knowledge only, without graph context
target_learners: K-12 students in Chinese primary, middle, and high school
target_learning_goals: Structural curriculum understanding: prerequisite reasoning, neighbor recommendation, experiment evidence chains, cross-chapter indexing
examples: A Prereq item asks which knowledge should be learned before Transposing Terms, with distractors sampled from structurally adjacent nodes such as taxonomic siblings
key_sources: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Mingrui Chen, Hengyi Feng, Zhaoyang Han, Xiaochen Ma, Zhen Hao Wong, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Wentao Zhang. (2026). K12-KGraph: A Curriculum-Aligned Knowledge Graph for Benchmarking and Training Educational LLMs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09635

article_title: K12-KGraph: A Curriculum-Aligned Knowledge Graph for Benchmarking and Training Educational LLMs
citation: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Mingrui Chen, Hengyi Feng, Zhaoyang Han, Xiaochen Ma, Zhen Hao Wong, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Wentao Zhang. (2026). K12-KGraph: A Curriculum-Aligned Knowledge Graph for Benchmarking and Training Educational LLMs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09635
title: K12-Train: a KG-guided QA synthesis pipeline yielding 7,335 educational SFT samples
description: K12-Train converts the knowledge graph into supervised fine-tuning data along three paths: node-grounded QA, edge-grounded QA with relation-specific question templates, and deterministic exercise-assessment templates. "The final dataset, K12-Train-Full, contains 7,335 QA pairs and is partitioned by modality according to whether answering requires visual input." K12-Train-Text contains 2,267 text-only pairs and K12-Train-MM contains 5,068 multimodal pairs, source-balanced to mitigate skew in the raw pool.
requirements: Edges are filtered by confidence threshold before prompting; QA pairs are validated for JSON structure, non-empty fields, and language consistency
constraints: Synthesized exclusively from the mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology subgraphs of the People's Education Press curriculum
target_learners: K-12 students in Chinese primary, middle, and high school
target_learning_goals: Curriculum content knowledge and structural relations between concepts, experiments, and figures
examples: Edge-grounded QA uses templates such as 'Why must one learn A before B?' for prerequisites_for and 'How does figure F explain concept C?' for illustrates
key_sources: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Mingrui Chen, Hengyi Feng, Zhaoyang Han, Xiaochen Ma, Zhen Hao Wong, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Wentao Zhang. (2026). K12-KGraph: A Curriculum-Aligned Knowledge Graph for Benchmarking and Training Educational LLMs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09635

article_title: Envisioning AI for K-12: What Should Every Child Know about AI?
citation: Touretzky, D.; Gardner-McCune, C.; Martin, F.; and Seehorn, D. (2019). Envisioning AI for K-12: What Should Every Child Know about AI? The Thirty-Third AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-19). https://www.aaai.org
title: Ecosystem of accessible AI tools for young K-12 programmers
description: The paper catalogs software and hardware tools that give young programmers AI components for their own creations: Cognimates Scratch extensions for speech and text categorization APIs, eCraft2Learn extensions for Snap!, Machine Learning for Kids classifier-training demos, the Cozmo robot with built-in computer vision, Calypso for Cozmo rule-based visual programming, Google AI experiments such as "Teachable Machine", Google AIY vision and voice kits, and TensorFlow Playground for exploring "neural networks and backpropagation learning". The authors argue students "need to be able to tinker with AI" to appreciate the big ideas.
requirements: Tools must make AI components accessible to young programmers within familiar environments like Scratch
target_learners: K-12 students, with some tools aimed at high school students and undergraduates
target_learning_goals: Hands-on experience with machine perception, machine learning, and robotics
examples: Machine Learning for Kids provides online demos where students train classifiers using web applications or Scratch extensions
key_sources: Touretzky, D.; Gardner-McCune, C.; Martin, F.; and Seehorn, D. (2019). Envisioning AI for K-12: What Should Every Child Know about AI? The Thirty-Third AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-19). https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33019795

article_title: Preface to the Special Issue on K-12 AI Education
citation: Ning Wang · James Lester. (2023). Preface to the Special Issue on K-12 AI Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00363-0
title: K-12 AI education as a distinct emerging field, analogous to science or history education
description: The editors frame "AI Education for K-12" as a field distinct from "AI in Education": whereas AIED has long built technologies to support human learning, this field educates K-12 students about AI itself. They write that "in a manner that is analogous to how we educate K-12 students about science or history, we now must develop curricula, pedagogies, and learning technologies" for K-12 AI education. The special issue is presented as a first step toward crystallizing this nascent research field.
requirements: Curricula, pedagogies, and learning technologies must be developed to support K-12 AI education, as the article states
key_sources: Ning Wang · James Lester. (2023). Preface to the Special Issue on K-12 AI Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00363-0

article_title: Comparison of the problem based learning-driven with the traditional didactic-lecture-based curricula.
citation: Zahid Muhammad A., Varghese Ramani, Mohammed Ahmed M., Ayed Adel K. (2016). Comparison of the problem based learning-driven with the traditional didactic-lecture-based curricula. International Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.5749.80f5
title: K1/K2 classification of multiple-choice questions by cognitive level
description: The article uses a two-type classification of single-best-answer MCQs based on the cognitive level they tap. K1 items require candidates to "recognize, remember, retrieve, identify, and recall a term", whereas K2 items require candidates "to select the reasons or identify the most correct explanation for the given clinical manifestations described in the question". The authors claim K2-type MCQs test depth, integration, analysis and application of knowledge in varied clinical situations, and use this classification to compare curricula. Items were categorized by independent subject experts serving as external examiners.
requirements: Independent subject experts to categorize items into K1 or K2 type
Items developed in accordance with a blueprint derived from weekly learning objectives
constraints: The authors state the K1/K2 categorization may have been relatively arbitrary due to academic staff bias
target_learning_goals: assessing higher-cognitive theoretical knowledge base in psychiatry
examples: Independent subject experts classified 104/225 (79.6%) of new-curriculum questions as K2 type and 144/220 (80.0%) of old-curriculum questions as K1 type
key_sources: Zahid Muhammad A., Varghese Ramani, Mohammed Ahmed M., Ayed Adel K. (2016). Comparison of the problem based learning-driven with the traditional didactic-lecture-based curricula. International Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.5749.80f5
